prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that shows practical wisdom: judgement about what to do in this situation, not just knowledge or passion.

passage_segments.text: I've read every study on four-day weeks published since 2015.
I also ran a three-month trial with my own team last year.
What I learned is that it works for project work but not for support desks, so I'd start with the product teams.
I'm passionate about work–life balance.

explanation_formal: Phronesis is practical judgement applied to particulars. Sentence 3 turns knowledge (1) and experience (2) into a situation-specific recommendation. Sentence 4 asserts a value (arete) rather than wisdom.
explanation_modern: Reading and doing aren't enough on their own. Sentence 3 shows you know when it works, when it doesn't, and where to start, and that's what makes people trust your call.

prompt_instruction: Click the Reluctant Conclusion: the point where the speaker argues against their own interest.

passage_segments.text: I'd love to tell you the tool my team built should replace the old one.
We spent eight months on it, and I'm proud of the work.
But the data says the old one handles edge cases better, so I recommend we keep it for another year.
Our users deserve the more reliable option.

explanation_formal: By declaring an interest (1–2) and then reaching a conclusion against it (3), the speaker demonstrates eunoia (disinterested goodwill), which heightens credibility for the recommendation.
explanation_modern: 'I wanted the opposite answer, but here's what the data says.' Nothing builds trust faster than a conclusion that costs you something.

prompt_instruction: The audience is a rural parish council. Click the sentence that builds ethos through shared values.

passage_segments.text: The broadband upgrade will cost the parish £40,000.
Like most of you, I've farmed here my whole life, and I don't spend money I can't account for.
The upgrade means three local businesses can stay instead of moving into town.
I'd ask you to approve it.

explanation_formal: Sentence 2 aligns the speaker's character with the audience's values (thrift, rootedness), which is arete. It answers in advance the suspicion that the spending is careless.
explanation_modern: 'I'm one of you, and I'm careful with money' lands before the ask. The £40,000 now comes from someone the room trusts.

passage_segments.text: I'll be upfront: I'm hopeless with spreadsheets, and the formatting in this report shows it.
But I spent three weeks on site interviewing every shift supervisor.
Every one of them named the same bottleneck: the loading dock schedule.
Fix that, and overtime costs drop.

options.text: Admitting a harmless weakness makes the claims that matter more believable.
options.feedback: Yes. Candour about something trivial buys credibility for the substance.

options.text: It lowers expectations, so any result looks good.
options.feedback: That's sandbagging. The flaw here doesn't touch the findings.
It's polite, but its job is strategic.

options.text: It doesn't work. Never admit weakness.
options.feedback: Admitting a weakness unrelated to your core claim reliably raises trust.

explanation_formal: The tactical flaw confesses a weakness irrelevant to the argument's substance, which signals candour and disarms scrutiny of the parts that matter.
explanation_modern: 'My spreadsheets are ugly' is a cheap thing to admit. It makes 'I interviewed every supervisor' sound even more solid.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence where the speaker raises an objection before anyone else can.

passage_segments.text: We should hold the planning week offsite at the converted barn.
Now, some of you will say the barn is too far for people with childcare to arrange.
So sessions will run from 10 to 3, with a minibus from the station.
The quiet will let us finish in four days what takes two weeks in the office.

explanation_formal: Procatalepsis anticipates an objection (2) and answers it (3) before the opponent can raise it, which shows foresight (phronesis) and removes the objection's force.
explanation_modern: Say their objection before they do and answer it. You look prepared, and they have nothing left to land.

prompt_instruction: Diagnose the CEO's move and choose the board member's reply.

passage_segments.text: Board member: “This acquisition is reckless.”
CEO: “It isn't reckless. It's bold.”
CEO: “Every company that leads its market took a risk like this once.”

steps.label: Figure
steps.question: What move does the CEO make in sentence 2?

options.text: Paradiastole: recasting a vice as its neighbouring virtue
options.feedback: Yes. 'Reckless' becomes 'bold' with the same facts and a kinder name.
No understatement by negation.
Nothing is anticipated. The objection has already been made.
Nothing is conceded.

options.text: It generalises from survivors and ignores firms that took similar risks and failed.
options.feedback: Right: a Bad Example (survivorship). The graveyard of bold failures is invisible.
No options are restricted.
It isn't circular, just badly sampled.
No denial is turned into evidence.
A label fight you can't win by repetition.

options.text: Bold or reckless, the question is the same: what's our downside if it fails, and can we cap it?
options.feedback: Refuses the naming contest and moves the stasis to policy and risk.
Ad hominem, and forensic.
Possibly relevant evidence, but on its own it reads as point-scoring about the past.

explanation_formal: Paradiastole redescribes the act under a neighbouring virtue. Its support commits survivorship bias. The effective counter declines the definitional contest and moves to deliberative risk assessment.
explanation_modern: Renaming the risk doesn't shrink it. Skip the word fight and ask the question either word leads to: how bad is the downside?

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence where the speaker turns the concession into an argument for their own position.

passage_segments.text: You're right that the new rota is unpopular. I've heard the complaints too.
And that unpopularity is exactly why we should fix the handover problems it exposed, rather than go back to a system that hid them.
Missed handovers have dropped from twelve a month to three.
Give it until March. If the numbers slip, we revisit.

explanation_formal: Paromologia: the opponent's point is granted (1) and then turned to the speaker's advantage (2). The concession becomes a premise for the speaker's conclusion.
explanation_modern: 'Yes, and that's why…' The complaint becomes your evidence. Then the speaker offers a fair test (sentence 4) so the concession doesn't feel like a trick.

prompt_instruction: The audience is engineers who dislike writing documentation. Click the commonplace the speaker builds on.

passage_segments.text: Most of us got into engineering because we hate doing the same work twice.
Undocumented code means someone has to rediscover how it works every single time.
So writing it down once is the lazy engineer's best friend.
I'm proposing a thirty-minute documentation slot at the end of every ticket.

explanation_formal: The speaker starts from a belief the audience already holds (aversion to repetition) and argues from it, rather than attacking their aversion to documentation directly.
explanation_modern: Don't fight what they believe. Use it. 'You hate repeating work' turns documentation from a chore into the lazy option.

prompt_instruction: You're the councillor. Read the room and respond.

passage_segments.text: Resident: “You people at the council don't care if our kids get run over!
Three near-misses outside the school this term, and you've done NOTHING!”

options.feedback: Yes: blame for past inaction, delivered hot.
No proposal, and no calm.
Very much not praise.
The near-misses are presented as fact, not in dispute.
Telling people to calm down reliably does the opposite.

options.text: Three near-misses outside a school is frightening, and you're right to be angry about it.
options.feedback: It validates the emotion and the fact, and the temperature drops.

options.text: Actually, the council has a strong safety record.
options.feedback: Defensive, and it reads as not listening.
Cold logos to a hot room. Worse than silence.

options.text: Here's what I can do this week: commission a speed survey and bring the crossing proposal to the committee on the 14th.
options.feedback: Concrete, near-term and deliberative. It gives the anger somewhere to go.

options.text: The previous councillor should have dealt with this.
options.feedback: Back into blame.
A demonstrative platitude with no action.
Vague, and exactly what they've heard before.

explanation_formal: Pathos must be lowered before logos can function: acknowledge the emotion's legitimacy, then redirect from forensic grievance to a specific deliberative commitment.
explanation_modern: First show you've heard them, then give them something real. Facts before feelings are acknowledged just bounce off.

prompt_instruction: Three openings from a migration planning meeting. Name the pillar of ethos each one leans on.

passage_segments.text: A: “I've led three of these migrations, and the one that failed taught me to freeze schema changes a month out.”
B: “Honestly, my team would gain most from option B, but option A is better for the company, so I'm backing A.”
C: “Like all of you, I believe our customers' data isn't ours to gamble with.”

options.feedback: Experience turned into a concrete rule of judgement.
Nothing is given up.
It's about know-how, not values.
No situational expertise is shown.
A reluctant conclusion against their own team's interest.
Close, but the tell is the sacrifice.
No expertise is claimed.
No interest is sacrificed.
'Like all of you, I believe…' aligns the speaker with the room's values.

explanation_formal: Aristotle's three sources of ethos (Rhetoric II.1): phronesis (practical wisdom), arete (virtue) and eunoia (goodwill, which Heinrichs recasts as disinterest).
explanation_modern: Know-how (A), 'this costs me, but…' (B), 'I'm one of you' (C). Strong speakers use all three, and the best pick the one this audience doubts most.

passage_segments.text: The council calls the new parking charges a “congestion measure”.
Let's call them what they are: a tax on people who can't afford to live in the centre.
Shift workers at the hospital have no bus that runs before 6 a.m.
At the very least, I'd ask the council to exempt hospital staff.

explanation_formal: Paradiastole redescribes the same measure under a less favourable heading ('tax' rather than 'congestion measure'). The redescription then frames the data and the proposal that follow.
explanation_modern: Whoever names the thing frames the fight. 'Congestion measure' sounds technical; 'a tax on the less well-off' sounds unfair. Notice it, and use it with care.
